qt: to the Commission Paolo Borchia (PfE) Subject:

The European Court of Auditors’ Annual Report has, for the seventh year in a row, issued a negative opinion concerning how the EU budget is being spent. The Report indicates that, in 2025, the estimated error rate in cohesion spending rose to 6.6 %, while the rate for agriculture and the environment climbed to 3.9 %. The ECA also drew attention to shortcomings in the implementation of the RRF, examples of which include non-compliant payments, unfulfilled objectives and breaches of public procurement rules. These findings are particularly relevant in the light of the Commission’s plans to introduce new own resources to bolster EU revenue, a measure that could result in additional burdens for citizens and businesses. Given the above: 1.
What concrete steps will the Commission take to remedy the shortcomings flagged up by the ECA and ensure that resources under the EU budget are managed in a more scrupulous and efficient manner?
Before it asks for additional own resources, how will the Commission prove to citizens that it can use EU resources in a rigorous, transparent and efficient manner?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.11.2026) The Commission strives to strike the right balance between a low level of error, fast payments, reasonable costs of controls and timely delivery on its policy objectives, by (i) promoting the use of simplified cost options, lump sums and financing not linked to costs; (ii) leveraging innovative tools to improve controls; (iii) providing guidance to Member States, training and capacity-building support; and (iv) ensuring that weaknesses in national control systems are addressed. Within this robust control framework, the Commission and Member States carry out thousands of checks annually to prevent, detect and correct errors and protect the EU budget. Through its Annual Management and Performance Report1, the Commission takes overall political responsibility for managing the EU budget. The report presents results achieved, internal control arrangements, financial management and measures to protect the EU’s financial interests. In addition, the European Court of Auditors provides independent scrutiny of the accounts, revenue and expenditure, as well as the performance of spending and policy areas. For the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework, the Commission has proposed a horizontal performance framework2, for tracking expenditure and measuring outputs and results across EU programmes. Harmonised indicators and streamlined reporting will make it easier to assess progress towards objectives while reducing administrative burden. A single gateway will provide a single point of access to information on EU budget implementation, performance and funding opportunities, strengthening transparency and public scrutiny. These measures will complement financial controls and corrective actions, helping to demonstrate how EU resources are used and what they deliver.
